title: Manassa Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Manassa wells have a 100-foot median depth; see local yields, water levels, permit history, and drilling costs.
h1: Manassa, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near Manassa means understanding the local well record before you rely on a driller’s estimate or a seller’s description. The Colorado DWR permit records within five miles show 1,022 wells, including 788 recorded as constructed. Those records point to generally moderate depths, strong reported yields, and shallow static water levels, but the data is not complete for every well.

Only 117 wells report a pump yield and 78 report a static water level. Treat the statistics as a planning guide, not a guarantee for a particular lot. Nearby Romeo, Sanford, La Jara, Conejos, and Antonito can provide useful comparison points, but the well on the property still matters most.

sections.heading: Manassa well depths and the ground below
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Manassa is 100 feet. The middle half runs from 50 to 120 feet, so many drilling bids should be based on a relatively shallow hole. Half of the recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 40% fall between 100 and 300 feet.

There is still meaningful variation. The 90th-percentile depth is 286 feet, and the deepest record reaches 929 feet. The permit aquifer descriptions include unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers for 742 wells, along with confined San Luis Valley aquifer descriptions on other records. Mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground supports a starting cost estimate, but changing materials or bedrock can move the final depth and price.

sections.heading: What a Manassa well may produce
sections.html:
Reported well yields are favorable in this record set, with a 15.0 gallons-per-minute median and a middle half from 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Of the wells reporting yield, 62% are above 15 gallons per minute and 38% are between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

No reported wells fall under 1 gallon per minute or between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. That does not eliminate the risk of a weak new well, because only 117 wells report a pump yield and the permit record does not test every property the same way. Ask for the completion report, pump test, storage setup, and intended household or stock use before assuming the well can support expansion or irrigation.

sections.heading: Water levels around Manassa and the recent trend
sections.html:
The median static water level is 18 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 10 to 40 feet. A shallow static level can simplify pumping, but it also makes proper casing, grouting, surface drainage, and septic planning important. Water quality and seasonal performance still need property-specific testing.

The decade figures show a median static level of 14 feet below ground in the 2010s and 18 feet in the 2020s. That is a deeper measured water level in the newer decade, but the records are limited to 78 reported measurements and may not compare identical wells or conditions. It is a reason to review nearby logs rather than claim a basin-wide decline from this series alone.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Manassa, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity extends across several generations. Records show 40 permits from the 1950s, 12 from the 1960s, 180 from the 1970s, 38 from the 1980s, 108 from the 1990s, 155 from the 2000s, 137 from the 2010s, and 88 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025, so this is not only an old-well area.

The most frequent driller names in the records are Heersink Drilling, also listed as Heersink, Scott, with 76 wells; Rocky Mountain Waterworks LLC, listed with Phythian, Donald L., with 49; and Valley Pump Company, listed with Self, Clinton L., with 48. These counts describe permit records, not a recommendation or a guarantee of current availability.

sections.heading: Manassa well drilling cost and finished-system budget
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground described for this area, the planning rate is $50 to $75 per foot. At the 100-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $5,000 to $7,500. That figure is for drilling, not a ready-to-use water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $11,000 to $19,500 at the median depth. A lot requiring a deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, or more trenching can exceed that range. Get the driller to state what depth is included, how overage is billed, and which pump, tank, electrical, and testing items are excluded.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
Well records near Manassa include 70% domestic or household use, 37% stock use, 13% irrigation use, and 2% monitoring use. Confirm that the existing permit and well construction match your intended use. A household well is not automatically an irrigation supply, and an exempt household-use well still has Colorado limits on pumping and use.

Environmental screening also matters. Within about 10 miles are 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site, 14 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those mapped sites do not prove contamination at a particular parcel, but they justify a water-quality test and a review of nearby land uses. Check septic setbacks, drainage, access for a rig, electrical routing, and the location of the proposed home before closing or drilling.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Manassa, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within five miles of Manassa is 100 feet. The middle half runs from 50 to 120 feet, while 40% are between 100 and 300 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 286 feet, and the deepest record is 929 feet, so a nearby log is more useful than relying on the median alone.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Manassa?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $75 per foot in mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 100-foot median depth, drilling is estimated at $5,000 to $7,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $11,000 to $19,500. Deeper drilling or difficult access can increase the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Manassa?
faq.a: Among the 117 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. The records show 62% above 15 gallons per minute and 38% between 5 and 15. These figures do not guarantee a new well’s performance, so request a pump test.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Manassa?
faq.a: The permit map cannot certify drinking-water safety. Within about 10 miles are 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site, 14 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Test the individual well for relevant contaminants, inspect its casing and grout, and review septic and nearby land uses before relying on it for household water.

faq.q: Are Manassa water levels getting lower?
faq.a: Reported static water levels have a median of 14 feet below ground in the 2010s and 18 feet in the 2020s. That suggests deeper measured water levels in the newer decade, but only 78 wells report a static level, and the measurements may not represent the same wells or conditions. Use nearby well logs and a current measurement for a property decision.
